title: The Iron Plough Farmers Feared, and the Barren Land at Kundal Road
dek: Laxmanrao Kirloskar spent two years selling his first iron ploughs, then lost his Belgaum workshop and began again on bare ground by a railway halt in 1910.

story.event: Restarting the plough works on barren land at Kundal Road after being ordered out of Belgaum
story.summary: Laxmanrao Kirloskar turned his family's Belgaum bicycle business towards manufacturing, making a chaff cutter in 1902 and an iron plough soon after, which farmers who feared iron would poison the soil took about two years to buy. When the Belgaum municipality ordered the workshop out to make room for a new suburb, the Raja of Aundh offered land and a loan, and in March 1910 the brothers restarted with 25 workers on barren land by Kundal Road station, later renamed Kirloskarvadi.
paragraphs: In the first years of the twentieth century Laxmanrao Kirloskar was trying to sell an iron plough to farmers around Belgaum, in what is now Karnataka, and they did not want it. Many believed iron would poison the soil and leave it useless. By the account in the Indian Posts and Telegraphs Department's folder for his 1969 centenary stamp, it took him two years to sell his first ploughs.

He had come to making things sideways. Born in 1869 in a village in Belgaum district, he taught at the Victoria Jubilee Technical Institute in Bombay and, Business Today reported, left after being denied a promotion. In Belgaum the family firm, Kirloskar Brothers, begun in 1888 and run at first by his brother Ramchandrarao, sold and repaired bicycles. Laxmanrao turned it from selling to manufacturing: a hand-powered chaff cutter in 1902, then the plough, dated 1903 by the company and 1905 by Business Today.

Then the workshop lost its ground. The Belgaum municipality ordered the Kirloskars to leave their premises to make room for a new suburb, in 1908 by Business Today's account and in January 1910 by a local history. The postal folder records that he could not find another suitable site. Balasaheb Pant Pratinidhi, the Raja of Aundh, offered land and a loan, ten thousand rupees according to the folder. The land was barren and lay beside a railway station called Kundal Road.

In March 1910 the brothers started again there with 25 workers. The station later took the name of the settlement that grew around the works, Kirloskarvadi. In that township, the postal folder records, Laxmanrao banned untouchability and employed former convicts as night watchmen. In Belgaum, the road where the bicycle shop stood is now named after him.

quote.text: The man who is rich in fancy thinks his waggon as good as built already—the fool! He does not know that there are a hundred timbers to a waggon. Take care to lay these up beforehand at home.
quote.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg eBook #348
quote.connection: Hesiod, a farmer writing for farmers, mocks the man who thinks his waggon built before he has gathered its hundred timbers. Kirloskar's second start was assembled from such pieces: a loan, a bare plot by a railway halt, twenty-five workers, and ploughs that farmers had taken two years to trust.

reflection: Two things in this story move slowly, and neither is a failure. Farmers took two years to trust iron in their soil; their fear was mistaken, but it was theirs, and it had to be met one field at a time. And when the workshop had to move, nobody rebuilt it in a season. It began again with twenty-five people and a plot of bare ground.
When something you are making is slow to be accepted, or has to start over somewhere less comfortable, it can feel like a verdict on you. Often it is only a count of the timbers still to be gathered.
invitation: Name one person whose doubt about your work you have been treating as an obstacle. Today, ask them one question about what worries them, and only listen to the answer.

research_notes: Dates disagree and the story gives the alternatives: the iron plough is 1903 on the group's legacy page and 1905 in Business Today (other timelines say 1901); the municipality's order is 1908 in Business Today and January 1910 on All About Belgaum. The loan is ten thousand rupees in the 1969 postal folder text (and All About Belgaum) but 17,000 rupees on Wikipedia; the story uses the folder's figure and attributes it. Who ran the 1888 shop: Business Today says Ramchandrarao ran a trading firm while Laxmanrao was in Bombay; the postal folder and the group page say Laxmanrao opened a cycle repair shop; the story says the firm was begun in 1888 and run at first by Ramchandrarao and sold and repaired bicycles. The '32 acres strewn with cacti and infested with cobras' appears only on the uncited All About Belgaum page, so the story says only that the land was barren (group page, folder). One copy of the folder (iStampGallery) says the two years were needed to sell the first six ploughs; the other copy does not give the number, so the story omits it. The postal folder is cited from a collector site's transcription that names the P&T information folder as its source; a second transcription on istampgallery.com agrees on the points used. No first-person account by Laxmanrao was found, so the story states no thoughts or feelings of his; Business Today's 'upset at being denied his rightful promotion' is reduced to the fact that he left after being denied promotion. The Economic Times centenary article (2010), an Indian Express story and two Business Standard articles load for the verifier but could not be read here, so they are not cited. Arc changed from the slate's change-of-direction to setback: the episode told is the forced move and restart; the earlier shift from bicycles to manufacturing is background. Funding kept as bootstrapped; the only outside money was the Raja's loan. Hesiod's lines are Works and Days 448-457 as numbered in Evelyn-White's translation.
